# Menopause & midlife health

> *Menopause changes a woman's body in real, specific ways, and it gets blamed for many changes it does
> not cause. The clinician's task is to tell the two apart, and to know which midlife problems a good diet
> helps and which it cannot touch.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Distinguish the menopause-linked shift of fat to the abdomen from the age-related rise in total weight.
- Interpret the evidence that energy expenditure, adjusted for fat-free mass, does not fall at menopause,
  and explain why preserving muscle beats hard dieting.
- Explain how falling oestrogen accelerates bone loss around the final menstrual period, and why mechanical
  loading does more than calcium and vitamin D supplements.
- Distinguish the menopause-linked step in LDL-cholesterol from the age-related drift in blood pressure and
  glucose.
- Evaluate claims about soy for hot flushes and breast-cancer risk, separating soy foods from isoflavone
  supplements.
- Recognise when a midlife problem needs investigation or referral instead of diet, and counsel
  weight-inclusively.
:::

## Menopause & midlife health at a glance: two drivers {#sec-overview}

**Menopause** is a reproductive transition rather than a disease: the ovaries wind down and oestrogen
falls. Three terms date the transition:

Final menstrual period (FMP)
: A woman's last menstrual period, the clinical reference point for dating menopause.

Perimenopause
: The years of fluctuating ovarian hormones before the FMP.

Postmenopause
: The years after the FMP.

In Singapore the mean age of natural menopause is about 49 years, with little difference across Chinese,
Malay and Indian women [@loh2005sgMenopause].

Menopause reshapes several nutrition-relevant systems at once, through the internal drivers and external
levers that frame every life stage (see the *Reading the life stages* chapter):

| Driver | What changes at this stage |
|---|---|
| Internal drivers (inside the body) | The fall in oestrogen, which changes bone, blood lipids and where fat is stored |
| External levers (life and environment) | The factors a woman and her clinician can change: physical activity, the food pattern, alcohol, and the "menopause" marketing she now meets |

In Western accounts hot flushes define menopause, but the local picture differs. In Singaporean surveys
the commonest complaints are aching joints and muscles and poor sleep, with hot flushes reported less often
[@chim2002sgSymptoms; @logan2023iwhp]. A woman here may never mention a flush, so listen for the aches and
the sleepless nights instead.

## What changes inside: weight, bone and the heart {#sec-meno-changes}

### Does menopause cause weight gain or slow the metabolism? {#sec-meno-weight}

Almost every woman reaches midlife having been told that menopause will make her gain weight and slow her
metabolism, and much midlife advice is built on those two beliefs. The cohort and energy-expenditure data
support neither in its usual form.

Total weight gain at midlife follows age and energy balance, not menopause. In women followed through the
transition, the scale rises steadily with age, with no jump timed to the FMP [@greendale2019swanBodyComp].
What menopause does change is where the fat sits. Around the FMP the rate of fat gain roughly doubles and
lean (muscle) mass falls [@greendale2019swanBodyComp], and fat shifts towards the abdomen, the visceral,
metabolically active depot (see the *Energy balance* chapter) [@lovejoy2008visceral]. The waistline, not the
scale, therefore shows the menopause-linked change.

Nor does energy expenditure fall sharply at menopause (see the *Adulthood* chapter for the
lifespan data). When total energy expenditure is measured properly and adjusted for fat-free mass, it is
stable from about age 20 to 60, through pregnancy and through menopause, and begins its slow decline,
about 0.7% a year, only after 60 [@pontzer2021energy]. Any fall in a woman's energy expenditure comes
mostly from losing muscle, and muscle is what resistance exercise and enough protein can preserve.

Both findings lead to the same advice: keep the muscle (protein plus resistance work) and mind the pattern
and the portions. Aggressive dieting works against keeping the muscle, because severe restriction speeds
the loss of lean mass and bone. The timeline below plots weight, fat and lean mass against the FMP; switch
its layers to see the bone and lipid changes described in [Bone](#sec-meno-bone) and
[The cardiometabolic shift](#sec-meno-heart).

<div data-island="menopause-timeline" data-src="/diagrams/menopause-timeline.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a woman's weight has barely changed since her final period, but her waist has grown. Why is the waist the better guide?
Total weight at midlife rises steadily with age and energy balance, with no jump at the final menstrual
period, so the scale shows little that is specific to menopause. What menopause changes is body
composition: around the FMP fat gain speeds up, lean mass falls, and fat moves to the abdomen, the visceral
depot. A growing waist on a stable weight is that menopause-linked shift.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: energy expenditure does not fall sharply at menopause. Why, then, does hard dieting backfire?
Adjusted for fat-free mass, total energy expenditure is stable from about 20 to 60, so any fall in a
woman's expenditure comes mostly from losing muscle. Protein and resistance exercise preserve that muscle.
Severe restriction does the opposite: it speeds the loss of lean mass and bone.
:::

### Bone: fast loss around the final menstrual period {#sec-meno-bone}

Bone is continually broken down and rebuilt throughout adult life. Two terms describe the process:

Bone remodelling
: The continual turnover of bone, in which old bone is broken down (resorption) and new bone is laid down
  (formation).

RANKL
: A signalling molecule that promotes bone resorption by osteoclasts (bone-resorbing cells); it rises when
  oestrogen falls.

Oestrogen normally inhibits bone resorption. When it falls, RANKL rises, osteoclasts become more
numerous and longer-lived, and resorption outpaces formation [@eghbali2003rankl]. Bone loss, gradual for
most of adult life, therefore accelerates sharply in a narrow window, from about a year before the FMP to
about two years after, reaching roughly 2% a year and removing around 7% of spine bone across the
transition [@greendale2012swanBone]. Chinese women, Singapore's majority, are among the groups that lose bone
faster through this window [@greendale2012swanBone].

Diet can supply bone's raw materials but cannot stop the oestrogen-driven loss. Calcium, vitamin D and
protein are permissive: remodelling needs them in adequate amounts, but they cannot halt the resorption.
Routine low-dose calcium-plus-vitamin-D supplements give no net fracture-prevention benefit in
community-dwelling women after menopause, and they slightly raise the risk of kidney stones
[@uspstfCalcium2018]. Supplements are therefore for a genuine shortfall or diagnosed osteoporosis (low bone
density that raises the risk of fracture).

A long-standing belief holds that protein "leaches" calcium from bone. With enough calcium, higher protein
intake instead tracks with better bone and fewer hip fractures [@groenendijk2019protein]. (Protein targets
are in the *Macronutrients* chapter, and sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle strength and mass, in
the *Healthy ageing* chapter.)

**Mechanical loading**, exercise that stresses the skeleton through impact or resistance, is the most
effective lifestyle measure for bone. In one small, supervised trial, progressive resistance
and impact training held or even modestly raised bone density where a home-based, low-intensity exercise programme did not
[@watson2018liftmor], a real but bounded effect. The everyday version is brisk walking or jogging plus
some strength work, not a prescription to self-load heavily.

At midlife the aim is to recognise the window and act early, protecting bone with food and loading before
the window closes. (The diagnosis and drug management of osteoporosis, and the calcium and vitamin D
reference intakes, are in the *Bone & joint health* chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out & 🍳 healthy kitchen: bone nutrients from food first
Local calcium is easier to find than it looks:

- Choose calcium-set tofu and *tau kwa*, and order *yong tau foo* with more beancurd.
- Keep ikan bilis and canned sardines (bones and all) in the kitchen.
- Add kai-lan and other low-oxalate Asian greens.
- Use calcium-fortified soy milk.

Pair the food with some sun and activity. Despite the climate, about one in three midlife Singaporean
women are deficient in vitamin D, because of indoor lives and sun avoidance, not a lack of sun; Indian and
Malay women are at higher risk [@cheong2021vitDsg]. Local calcium intakes sit at or below target, so food
first is a realistic strategy [@hpbNNS2010].
:::

### The cardiometabolic shift: which changes are menopause-linked {#sec-meno-heart}

Before menopause, women have a cardiovascular "advantage" over men, and the transition erodes it. The
change is selective. LDL-cholesterol and **apolipoprotein B** (apoB, the protein carried on each LDL
particle) rise in a sharp step right around the FMP, so that change is menopause-linked; blood pressure,
glucose and triglycerides drift up with age, not with the FMP [@matthews2009swanLipids]. Visceral fat and
the incidence of the metabolic syndrome also climb through the transition [@janssen2008swanMetS]. An
American Heart Association scientific statement treats midlife as a window for early prevention of
cardiovascular disease in women [@elkhoudary2020ahaMenopause].

Separating the menopause-linked changes from the age-related ones guards against two opposite errors. One
is over-attribution ("everything bad at midlife is menopause", when the blood pressure is probably
ageing); the other is under-attribution ("nothing has changed", when the LDL-cholesterol step and the
visceral fat are real). The dietary intervention is a whole dietary pattern, Mediterranean- or DASH-style,
in place of single nutrients (see the *What a healthy diet looks like* chapter). The midlife task is to
start the pattern early, before the numbers go wrong. (The management of lipids and blood pressure is in
the *Cardiovascular disease & hypertension* chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a 50-year-old already takes calcium and vitamin D. Why will that not stop the bone loss around her final period, and what does more?
The loss is driven by falling oestrogen: RANKL rises, osteoclasts become more numerous and longer-lived,
and resorption outpaces formation. Calcium, vitamin D and protein are permissive raw materials for
remodelling, so they cannot stop that oestrogen-driven loss, and routine low-dose supplements give no net
fracture benefit in community-dwelling women after menopause. Mechanical loading, through resistance and
impact exercise, is the most effective lifestyle measure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: blood pressure and glucose only drift up with age. Why is midlife still treated as a window for preventing heart disease in women?
Some changes are menopause-linked: LDL-cholesterol and apoB step up sharply around the FMP, and visceral
fat and the incidence of the metabolic syndrome climb through the transition. Those changes erode women's
cardiovascular advantage over men, adding to the age-related drift, so a whole dietary pattern started
early acts before the numbers go wrong.
:::

## What changes outside: soy foods and the supplement marketplace {#sec-meno-soy-limits}

No midlife topic attracts more marketing than soy and its **phytoestrogens**, plant compounds that weakly
mimic oestrogen (in soy, chiefly the **isoflavones**). The popular story errs in both directions: it
overstates soy's benefit for hot flushes and overstates its risk for breast cancer.

### Soy and hot flushes: at most a modest, inconsistent effect {#sec-meno-soy}

For hot flushes, soy does less than the marketing claims. Pooled trials of isoflavone supplements show at
most a modest and inconsistent reduction in flushes, around a fifth fewer, an effect far weaker and slower
than that of **menopausal hormone therapy** (prescribed hormones that replace the oestrogen the ovaries no
longer make) [@taku2012isoflavones; @chen2015phyto]. The highest-quality synthesis, a
Cochrane review, finds no reliable benefit overall, with a signal only for extracts high in genistein, one
of the soy isoflavones [@lethaby2013cochranePhyto].

Part of the inconsistency is biological. Only some people (more in Asian populations) carry the gut
bacteria that convert a soy isoflavone into **equol**, its more active form [@setchell2002equol]. Giving
equol directly to non-producers helped in one small placebo-controlled trial, a preliminary finding [@aso2012sequol]. On the pooled evidence, the
North American Menopause Society does not recommend soy foods, soy extracts or equol as a treatment for
flushes [@namsNonhormone2023]. The line to give a patient: *soy foods are a fine, healthy part of your diet,
but they are not hormone therapy and I would not count on them to fix the flushes.*

### Safety: soy and breast-cancer risk {#sec-meno-soy-safety}

On safety, soy is feared more than the evidence supports. Many women have heard that soy "causes breast
cancer" or "feeds" oestrogen-sensitive tumours, a fear that came from rodent studies that do not translate
to humans. In people, and especially at the habitual Asian intakes relevant here, soy foods are associated
with lower breast-cancer risk [@wu2008soyMeta]. They are also safe for survivors, including women with
**oestrogen-receptor-positive** (oestrogen-sensitive) disease and those taking **tamoxifen** (an
anti-oestrogen drug used to treat it); if anything, survivors who eat moderate soy do better
[@shu2009shanghai; @nechuta2012abcpp]. The reassurance is for whole soy foods, not for high-dose
isoflavone pills, which are a different and less-tested product.

(The appraisal toolkit for tracing claims such as "soy fixes menopause" or "soy causes cancer" back to
the underlying evidence is in the *Evidence vs hype* chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out: soy is on every hawker menu
Singapore's everyday soy foods are the foods in the studies that link soy to lower breast-cancer risk at
local intakes [@wu2008sgSoy]: *tau huay* and soybean milk, *tauhu* and *tau kwa*, *tau pok*, *foo chok*
(beancurd skin), tempeh and edamame. Enjoy them as good, protein-rich food, but don't sell them, or buy
them, as a flush cure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why is soy reasonable to offer as food but not as a treatment for hot flushes?
Soy foods are safe and, at Asian intakes, linked to lower breast-cancer risk, so there is no reason to
avoid them. As a treatment, isoflavone supplements reduce flushes only modestly and inconsistently, partly
because only some people's gut bacteria convert isoflavones into equol, the more active form. The North
American Menopause Society therefore does not recommend soy as a flush treatment.
:::

## Recognising trouble, and when to refer {#sec-meno-refer}

Some midlife problems lie beyond what diet can do, and some popular remedies do harm. Patients are most
easily exploited where diet reaches its limits.

### When nutrition is not the answer {#sec-meno-limits}

Three problems mark the limits of diet:

- After periods stop, iron needs fall, and a new deficiency is a red flag. Requirements drop to about the
  level of an adult man's, so routine iron supplements become unnecessary, and there is no regulated
  pathway for excreting excess iron [@odsIron]. New iron-deficiency anaemia in a woman past menopause is
  therefore not a life-stage need to top up. It points to blood loss, usually gastrointestinal, and should
  be investigated, not self-treated.
- Vaginal and urinary symptoms have no dietary fix. The **genitourinary syndrome of menopause** (vaginal
  dryness and urinary symptoms) is common locally [@chim2002sgSymptoms], and no food or supplement treats
  it. Recognise it, and refer for effective therapy (moisturisers, topical oestrogen). Be alert to
  "natural remedy" marketing that targets exactly this symptom.
- Poor sleep, one of the top local complaints [@logan2023iwhp], responds to low-cost lifestyle measures:
  limiting alcohol (it fragments sleep), keeping caffeine to earlier in the day, avoiding large late meals, and
  minding weight. Sleep disrupted by night sweats or low mood may need referral instead of a dietary
  change.

### Unproven remedies and restrictive dieting {#sec-meno-harm}

A nightly glass of "wine for the flushes" is poor advice. Alcohol raises breast-cancer risk with no safe
threshold [@hamajima2002alcohol] and worsens both sleep and bone, so it is never a symptom remedy. There
is also no menopause-specific diet pill, and most "menopause supplements" are unproven (obesity medicines
are in the *Obesity & metabolic syndrome* chapter).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do no harm: restrictive dieting at midlife
Restrictive dieting and disordered eating occur in women aged 40–60 [@mangweth2014ed], so doing no harm
means counselling weight-inclusively and with consent. That counselling is anchored on protein, activity
and a sound pattern, not on weight loss, because severe restriction speeds the loss of lean mass and bone
(see [Does menopause cause weight gain or slow the metabolism?](#sec-meno-weight)). The *how* of the
conversation is in the *Behaviour-change counselling* chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does new iron-deficiency anaemia in a woman past menopause call for investigation?
Once periods stop, iron requirements fall to about an adult man's, and there is no regulated pathway for
excreting excess iron, so a new deficiency is not a life-stage need. It points to blood loss, usually
gastrointestinal, so the source needs investigating instead of a top-up.
:::

## Is there a "menopause diet"? {#sec-close}

No, and promising one does a disservice, because what diet and activity can do depends on the problem:

::: {.spectrum}
[What diet and activity do for midlife problems]{.tree-title}

- Vaginal dryness: nothing; refer
- Hot flushes: a little
- Bone and heart: a lot

[Nothing]{.spectrum-end} [A lot]{.spectrum-end}
:::

Diet and activity protect bone (food-first minerals plus loading) and the heart (a sound pattern, started
early), and a weight-inclusive approach avoids the harm of crash dieting.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Singapore is unusually well studied here, and four local findings change the counselling:

- Menopause arrives a little earlier than the Western figure of about 51 [@gold2001swanAge] (mean about 49 years here), and its symptoms differ:
  aches and broken sleep dominate over flushes, and Indian women report the heaviest symptom burden and
  Chinese women the least [@loh2005sgMenopause; @logan2023iwhp].
- Bone risk is higher than the sunshine suggests: bone loss through the transition is fast in Chinese
  women, Singapore's majority, and vitamin D deficiency is common [@greendale2012swanBone;
  @cheong2021vitDsg].
- The soy finding is local too: at the high habitual intakes of Asian diets, soy tracks with lower
  breast-cancer risk [@wu2008sgSoy].
- Menopause is often met with cultural silence, so the clinician frequently has to open the subject gently
  and normalise it.

Singapore now has its own menopause management guidelines [@kkh2026menopauseGuidelines] to refer to when symptoms outrun what nutrition and
lifestyle can do.
